# Rules

<!-- Generated by `manifestvet rules --markdown`; edit the rule in
     `src/manifestvet/rules.py` and regenerate. tests/test_docs.py enforces this. -->

40 rules (2 critical, 9 high, 17 medium, 9 low, 3 note). Every one has a sample manifest that triggers it
(`manifestvet demo` asserts the coverage).

Stages run in order: **element** rules look at one node, **component** rules at one
component and its intent-filters, **app** rules at the whole manifest.

## MVT001

**Application is debuggable** -- critical, stage 1 (element)

android:debuggable="true" leaves the JDWP agent on. Any process that can reach the device over adb can attach a debugger, read heap memory (tokens, decrypted payloads) and use run-as to read the app's private directory. Play rejects it, so seeing it in a shipped APK means the artifact was built or repacked outside the release pipeline.

**Fix.** Remove android:debuggable, or gate it on a build type (debuggable true only in debug).

## MVT037

**Exported component is gated by a permission any app can hold** -- critical, stage 3 (app)

The component declares a guard, so it reads as protected -- but the guard is a normal or dangerous permission, either a platform one (INTERNET, VIBRATE) or one this app declares at that level. Any app can request it and be granted at install. This is the most common false sense of security in Android manifests.

**Fix.** Guard with a signature-level permission, or set exported="false" and pass data over a Binder interface with a caller check (getCallingUid).

## MVT003

**Backup on with nothing excluded** -- high, stage 1 (element)

allowBackup="true" with neither fullBackupContent nor dataExtractionRules means every file under the app's data directory is in scope -- including token caches, databases and anything written to no_backup/ by mistake.

**Fix.** Set allowBackup="false", or point dataExtractionRules at a rules file that excludes credential caches and no_backup is used for the rest.

## MVT007

**sharedUserId declared** -- high, stage 1 (element)

A shared UID puts this app and every other app with the same userId into one sandbox: same data dir, same process namespace, same permissions. It is deprecated since API 29 and can never be removed later without breaking the install.

**Fix.** Remove sharedUserId and pass data between the apps over a content provider or a bound service.

## MVT013

**Exported activity with no permission** -- high, stage 1 (element)

Any installed app can start an exported activity with an explicit Intent and hand it arbitrary extras. If it is a settings screen, a WebView wrapper or a file picker, that is a confused-deputy path into the app's own privileges.

**Fix.** Set android:exported="false", or require a signature-level permission.

## MVT014

**Exported service with no permission** -- high, stage 1 (element)

A third-party app can bind or start the service and then call every public method on its Binder interface, in this app's UID, with this app's permissions.

**Fix.** Set android:exported="false", or bind behind a signature-level permission.

## MVT015

**Exported receiver with no permission** -- high, stage 1 (element)

An exported receiver takes broadcasts from any app. The payload is attacker-controlled and lands in onReceive before any validation, which is how state machines get driven into states the developer never wrote.

**Fix.** Set android:exported="false" unless another app must reach it, and guard with a signature permission if so.

## MVT016

**Exported provider with no read/write permission** -- high, stage 1 (element)

The provider answers content:// queries from any app. Without readPermission / writePermission the only thing between another app and the data is the provider's own URI matching -- and `content://authority/` plus a guessed path is a very short guess.

**Fix.** Set android:exported="false", or declare readPermission and writePermission at signature level.

## MVT018

**Provider grants URI permissions** -- high, stage 1 (element)

grantUriPermissions="true" lets a caller pass a content:// URI to a third app and have that app receive access too. Without a permission on the provider, that is a transferable capability: one leaked URI reads the file from anywhere.

**Fix.** Drop grantUriPermissions, or pair it with path-permission entries that scope the grantable paths.

## MVT019

**Provider path rule covers the whole tree** -- high, stage 1 (element)

A <path-permission path="/"> or <grant-uri-permission pathPrefix="/"> entry applies to every path under the authority. Paired with an export, it is the classic ../ traversal: the provider asks the filesystem for the joined path and hands back whatever it resolves to.

**Fix.** Narrow the path to the subtree that is shared, and validate the resolved path against a canonical prefix.

## MVT038

**Two providers share an authority** -- high, stage 3 (app)

Authorities are unique per device. Two providers claiming the same one means the second never installs, or -- worse -- one of them silently answers queries meant for the other. In a plugin/feature-module setup this is how a staging authority ships to production.

**Fix.** Give each provider a distinct authority derived from the application id and the module.

## MVT002

**Backup enabled by default** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

Below targetSdk 31, android:allowBackup defaults to true. `adb backup` then writes the app's private files into an archive the user (or anything holding the backup transport) can read offline, which is the cheapest way to lift stored sessions.

**Fix.** Declare android:allowBackup="false", or scope the backup with dataExtractionRules.

## MVT004

**Cleartext traffic explicitly allowed** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" re-enables plaintext HTTP for every host the app talks to, including third-party SDKs. On a hostile network that turns every API call into a readable, modifiable request.

**Fix.** Drop the flag, or scope cleartext to specific dev hosts in a networkSecurityConfig domain-config.

## MVT005

**Cleartext allowed by platform default** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

Before targetSdk 28 cleartext is permitted unless blocked. The manifest does not say so, which is why this is easy to miss in review: nothing in the file looks wrong.

**Fix.** Raise targetSdk to 28+, or set usesCleartextTraffic="false" explicitly.

## MVT008

**minSdkVersion below 21** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

Below API 21 the platform has no ART, no per-app SELinux domain per UID and no modern TLS stack. Every library the app ships then has to carry its own fallbacks, and the old code paths are the ones nobody tests.

**Fix.** Raise minSdkVersion to at least 21 (24+ if the dependency graph allows it).

## MVT009

**targetSdkVersion below 31** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

targetSdk gates which mitigations the platform applies. Below 31 the app keeps the permissive defaults for android:exported, mutable PendingIntents and unscoped backups -- the three things this tool reports on most often.

**Fix.** Raise targetSdkVersion to the current Play requirement (34+ as of 2026).

## MVT010

**targetSdkVersion not declared** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

Without targetSdkVersion the platform assumes the oldest behaviour it still supports, so every compatibility shim stays on. It is also the one field Play refuses to publish without, which makes its absence a sign of a hand-built APK.

**Fix.** Declare targetSdkVersion in <uses-sdk> (or via the Gradle targetSdk).

## MVT011

**<uses-sdk> missing entirely** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

No <uses-sdk> at all means minSdk 1 and targetSdk 1: the app claims to run on API 1 and opts out of every behavioural change since. Nothing else in the manifest can be judged against an API level, so the rest of this report is guesswork.

**Fix.** Add <uses-sdk android:minSdkVersion=... android:targetSdkVersion=...> (normally Gradle does this).

## MVT020

**Provider without authorities** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

A <provider> with no android:authorities cannot be addressed at all: the install fails, or the element is dead weight. Either way it is a manifest that no build actually validated.

**Fix.** Declare android:authorities="${applicationId}.provider" or delete the element.

## MVT021

**Exported activity uses a hijackable launch mode** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

singleTask / singleInstance activities are matched by taskAffinity as well as by class name. A malicious app that declares the same affinity can have its activity placed at the root of this app's task (StrandHogg 2.0), so the user sees the real app's UI on top of the attacker's screen.

**Fix.** Keep exported activities at standard launchMode, or set an empty taskAffinity and check `dumpsys activity`.

## MVT023

**Web deep link without autoVerify** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

An http/https filter without android:autoVerify leaves the link unverified, so any installed app can register the same host and win the intent. The user taps a link to your domain and lands in someone else's UI, prefilled with your URL.

**Fix.** Add android:autoVerify="true" and publish /.well-known/assetlinks.json for the host.

## MVT024

**Deep link matches every host** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

android:host="*" matches any host, so the filter is not a link into your app -- it is a claim on every URL of that scheme. Depending on the intent, the system may route unrelated links here, and a hostile app can use the same wildcard to intercept yours.

**Fix.** Name the specific host (and subdomains) the app serves.

## MVT025

**Deep link matches the whole path** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

pathPrefix="/" or pathPattern=".*" accepts any path under the host, so the app becomes the handler for pages it has no business rendering. Whatever the handler does with the trailing path (WebView.loadUrl is the usual) is now attacker-chosen input.

**Fix.** Match the concrete paths the app serves, and validate the path again inside the handler.

## MVT026

**Custom-scheme deep link into an exported activity** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

A custom scheme (myapp://) is first-come-first-served: any app can register the same string. When the target activity is exported and unguarded, the link is a way for another app to drive this one's UI with chosen parameters.

**Fix.** Treat custom-scheme parameters as untrusted input, and keep the handler activity unexported where possible.

## MVT029

**Exported receiver for a protected system broadcast** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

The platform delivers protected broadcasts (BOOT_COMPLETED, PACKAGE_ADDED, ...) to non-exported receivers too -- the protection is on the sender. Setting exported="true" adds nothing for these actions except a way for other apps to send them anyway.

**Fix.** Set android:exported="false" on receivers that only listen to system broadcasts.

## MVT030

**Intent filter action is not qualified** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

Action strings share one global namespace. A reverse-domain action (com.example.app.SYNC) is implicitly owned; a bare word (SYNC, UPDATE, PING) is owned by whoever registers it first, and any app can declare the same string with a higher priority to intercept the implicit intent.

**Fix.** Qualify every custom action with the application id (or the fully qualified class name).

## MVT031

**App-defined permission is normal-level** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

A permission declared with protectionLevel normal (the default) is granted to any app that asks for it at install time, silently. If it is meant to protect a component, the protection is decorative.

**Fix.** Use protectionLevel="signature" for permissions that gate components.

## MVT034

**Requests a permission it can never hold** -- medium, stage 1 (element)

Signature and privileged permissions are only granted to apps signed with the platform key or preinstalled in the system image. A third-party app that declares them gets no error and no grant -- the feature silently degrades, and the manifest reads as if the capability were there.

**Fix.** Remove the request, and reach the capability through a bound service, an accessibility service or a user-granted role instead.

## MVT006

**Legacy external storage requested** -- low, stage 1 (element)

requestLegacyExternalStorage keeps the pre-scoped-storage view of /sdcard alive. Any other app holding READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE can read whatever this app writes there -- the classic way a downloaded file leaks to every file manager on the device.

**Fix.** Move to scoped storage (MediaStore / app-specific dirs) and drop the flag.

## MVT017

**Exported activity with no intent-filter** -- low, stage 1 (element)

Exported with no filter means the activity is reachable only by an explicit Intent naming its class -- still reachable, since class names are in the APK, but the attacker has to know the name. Usually this is an android:exported left at true by copy-paste rather than a deliberate decision.

**Fix.** Set android:exported="false" if nothing outside the app is meant to start it.

## MVT022

**allowTaskReparenting enabled** -- low, stage 1 (element)

allowTaskReparenting lets the system move the activity into another task whose affinity matches. On its own it is a UX feature; combined with a shared affinity it is the other half of a task-hijack chain.

**Fix.** Remove android:allowTaskReparenting unless the reparenting is intentional.

## MVT028

**<data> scheme without host** -- low, stage 1 (element)

A scheme on its own (no host, no path) matches every URI with that scheme. For http that means the app claims to handle the entire web; for a custom scheme it means any shape of input reaches the handler.

**Fix.** Add android:host and a path constraint to every <data> that carries a scheme.

## MVT032

**App-defined permission has no protectionLevel** -- low, stage 1 (element)

protectionLevel is not inherited from anywhere; omitting it means normal. The omission reads as "I forgot" and is a reliable sign the permission was never threat-modelled.

**Fix.** Always write protectionLevel explicitly, even when it is normal.

## MVT035

**Requests an undefined permission** -- low, stage 1 (element)

A permission name that is neither a platform permission nor declared by this app is ignored at install. It is almost always a typo (READ_SMS vs READ_SMSS), and the code that depends on it fails a permission check at runtime instead of at review time.

**Fix.** Fix the name, or declare the permission in this manifest if it is app-defined.

## MVT036

**Requests QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES** -- low, stage 1 (element)

QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES turns the app into an inventory of everything installed -- a fingerprinting primitive, and a Play policy violation unless the app's core purpose needs it.

**Fix.** Replace it with a <queries> block naming the specific packages or intent shapes the app talks to.

## MVT039

**Component guard names a permission that does not exist** -- low, stage 3 (app)

android:permission pointing at a name neither the platform nor this app defines is silently ignored: the component ends up effectively unguarded while reading as guarded. Typos here survive review precisely because the line looks right.

**Fix.** Correct the permission name, or declare the permission in this manifest.

## MVT040

**Exported component runs in a global process** -- low, stage 3 (app)

A process name without a leading colon (android:process="com.example.shared") is global: any other app with the same sharedUserId and process name joins it. Memory in that process is then shared with code this app does not control.

**Fix.** Use a per-app private process (android:process=":remote") when isolation is the point.

## MVT012

**android:exported missing where the platform requires it** -- note, stage 1 (element)

Since API 31 a component that declares an intent-filter must declare android:exported; the build fails otherwise. A manifest in that state has been repacked by something that does not run the real checks, which is worth knowing before trusting the rest of it.

**Fix.** Add the explicit android:exported value that matches the intent.

## MVT027

**BROWSABLE filter with no data** -- note, stage 1 (element)

BROWSABLE without any <data> element cannot match a URL: the category promises link handling the filter cannot deliver. Harmless at runtime, but it hides the real filter in review.

**Fix.** Add the <data> elements the filter is meant to match, or drop the BROWSABLE category.

## MVT033

**App-defined permission is dangerous-level** -- note, stage 1 (element)

A dangerous permission shows the user a runtime prompt. For an app-defined permission that prompt explains nothing, so users grant it to make the dialog go away -- and any app that asks gets the same grant.

**Fix.** Reserve dangerous level for permissions that map to real user-visible capability, otherwise use signature.
